extracted.intended_audience: biomedical researchers (PIs, postdocs, trainees) interested in grants, publishing, and lab data practices
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of blog posts giving practical, norm-based guidance for researchers on journal metrics (JIF), data curation and sharing, preprints and journal/NIH policies, program evaluation for diversity efforts, and the role of grant funding in careers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal Impact Factor (JIF) calculation and what citations count
rubrics_metrics.description: “the impact factor of a journal is calculated by dividing the number of current year citations to the source items published in that journal during the previous two years” — JIF counts citations in the second and third calendar years after publication, and does not include the first calendar year of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether your paper would have boosted a journal's JIF, focus on citations in the second and third calendar years after publication (either individually or averaged). Ignore the first calendar year when doing this analysis. Use those years to compare your paper's citation performance to the journal median.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of JIF-based analysis for internal morale, not as persuasive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative comparison of your paper's citations to a rejecting journal's JIF is useful primarily for personal validation (fighting Imposter Syndrome), not for convincing editors or external audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if your paper outpoints a journal's JIF, editors will likely continue to make subjective judgments about what 'belongs' in their journal. Use JIF comparisons for your own assessment of impact rather than expecting it to change editorial behavior or serve as effective external bragging material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance data curation effort against cost and likely future utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every data point or study needs full curation/analysis/graphical depiction; data should be curated 'to the extent that it makes sense' because comprehensive curation has non-trivial time and opportunity costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize curation for data likely to be useful in the future or required by collaborators/funders. Expect many datasets to be 'used at need' rather than exhaustively curated; avoid expending disproportionate effort on low-value archival curation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid locking analysis in a single person's proprietary code; document and share analysis workflows
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis approaches should not be captive to a single trainee's laptop or proprietary software; ensure analyses can be reproduced and used by others in the lab.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate individual analyses into shared, maintainable programs; provide documentation so techs and trainees can run standard analyses. Use 'belt-and-suspenders' approaches to avoid loss of capability if a single person leaves. Strive for consistent output definitions across years (e.g., how a basic outcome is computed).

rubrics_metrics.name: PI-level requirements: consistency and rapid inspectability of lab data
rubrics_metrics.description: PIs need some orthodoxy in data structures, formats, analyses, and graphs so they can understand and quickly produce preliminary figures from past experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish consistent data conventions and graphing standards across the lab to enable quick checks and to prevent confusion over time. Accept that enforcing orthodoxy requires ongoing effort and occasional remediation of shortcuts taken by staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: External data curation/sharing has real costs and may be constrained by grant terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparing data for external users (open-data requesters, other researchers, private companies) requires staff time and resources and may conflict with grant-funded responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat requests for curation or bespoke data formatting as work that consumes grant-funded staff time; evaluate whether it aligns with funded aims and institutional rules. If the work is unrelated to the grant's aims, providing unpaid labor to third parties may violate grant rules or be otherwise inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider ownership, credit, and misuse risks before broad data sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about sharing all raw data should account for ownership, potential bad actors, academic credit, and opportunity costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh benefits of openness against risks (e.g., misuse by anti-science actors, loss of credit/opportunity). Sharing valuable, well-annotated subsets that serve collaborators may be preferable to publishing everything uncurated for unknown internet users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal preprint policies and disclosure requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals (e.g., JAMA titles) discourage public dissemination via preprint servers and will consider preprint postings in evaluating submissions; they require authors to disclose any preprint postings, provide copies, and links at submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before submitting, check the journal's policy on preprints. If a preprint exists, disclose it and provide copies/links as required. Be aware journals may deem a submission redundant with a preprint and may factor that into accept/reject decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of citations: Introduction vs Discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations to work published after your manuscript was written should generally go in the Discussion rather than the Introduction, because the Introduction should reflect what motivated the study at the time it was written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a new paper appeared while your manuscript was in revision and you did not perform new experiments motivated by it, discuss it in the Discussion (context/interpretation). Only add such citations to the Introduction if you actually performed new experiments for revision that were motivated by the newly published paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate diversity/pipeline programs with robust, representative outcome measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Program claims (e.g., 'helped foster careers') must be backed by comprehensive outcome data (faculty placements, longitudinal tracking); small, low-response surveys risk survivorship bias and overclaiming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require high coverage and transparent reporting (response rates, how 'reached' was defined) when assessing program impact. Beware of accepting 'largely stayed within academia' claims based on small, self-selected respondent pools; calculate outcomes relative to the total cohort, not only respondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mix award types when analyzing funding disparities; treat awards by type/value separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregating heterogeneous NIH award types (R01s, conference awards, small training or resource grants) into a single 'grant money' metric can produce misleading conclusions because different awards have very different career value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying disparities or evaluating career impact, separate analyses by award mechanism and consider career-relevance (e.g., R01 vs R21 vs conference award). Avoid conclusions that collapse all award dollars into equivalent signals of career advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH policy on preprints: applicants should label them; reviewers have discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH allows citing preprints in grant applications but distinguishes interim products from peer-reviewed publications and expects applicants to label them as not peer-reviewed; reviewers are not instructed to treat preprints as equivalent to peer-reviewed work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite preprints in applications and explicitly identify them as such. Advocate for their value via narrative/Rigor sections and by using them routinely. Expect reviewers to vary in how they treat preprints — some may discount them entirely while others may treat them like peer-reviewed papers; this is within reviewer discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant funding track record is a dominant evaluation metric in hiring and career progression
rubrics_metrics.description: A candidate's history of acquiring grant money and demonstrating ability to secure and deploy funding is a key predictor used by hiring committees and influences career opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a steady pipeline of grant submissions; prioritize obtaining and documenting grant support. Recognize that grant dollars often translate directly into employability and institutional decisions — money 'talks' in academic hiring and advancement.
